newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols off highs as spot bounces.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols off highs as spot bounces.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options slipped in late U.S. trading from early highs as the spot greenback bounced back from psychological support levels, dealers said.
Options trading was quiet in most currency pairs, due in part to caution ahead of Tuesday's U.S. elections, they added.

Dollar/yen volatilities rose early in the session when the U.S. unit threatened to break below 113.00 yen. But they soon retreated as the dollar clawed back up toward 114.00 yen, where it stalled again, well short of last week's highs.

"Volatilities opened up well bid in the morning with spot at 113.10," said a European bank trader in Chicago. "And then as spot settled in up here at 113.85, volatilities came off -- the whole curve has come off about 0.1-0.15 (point)."
For the options market, he added, time-decay was outweighing the event risk for Tuesday's elections.

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen options stood at 8.1/8.3 percent, up about 0.2 point from Friday but off a touch from early highs. Risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, were virtually unchanged, with one-month 25-delta assessed at 0.1/0.3 percent.
Mark/yen volatilities edged up as spot stayed firm in the mid-75 yen area, just below last week's highs. One-month dollar/mark gained 0.2 point to 7.3/7.6 percent.
Dollar/mark volatilities were little changed as spot drifted directionlessly in the 1.5080-1.5150 area, pushed around by cross activities in mark/yen, sterling/mark and mark/Swiss franc.
"Dollar/mark spot doesn't have a mind of its own," said Ted Voorhees, a senior trader at Deutsche Bank in New York.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark was about a tenth of a point off late Friday levels at 7.55/7.75 percent.

Good buying interest was seen in at-the-money options in the back end earlier in the day, while some very short-dated options were sought later in the day, probably in a strategy linked to the U.S. elections, traders said.

Sterling volatilities, although not very liquid in U.S. trading, were firmer bid as spot cable rallied in the wake of news British Telecommunications PLC was merging with MCI Communications Corp in what could be a $20 billion deal.
Spot cable fell on Friday after talk of the merger first surfaced, but bounced back strongly as the story unfolded.
"It's added a little volatility -- not directional, but just general volatility," the Chicago trader said.
"People were caught napping with cable...and it seems that panic takes place more and more every day," added Voorhees at Deutsche Bank.
One-month cable volatility stood at 8.3/8.7 percent versus 8.1/8.6 at European midsession and 7.6/8.2 late on Friday.
